# AI Instructions for dotfiles Repository

# Repository Overview

This repository defines a reproducible NixOS and Home Manager setup through Nix flakes.
It includes a Python CLI, Neovim (LazyVim), tmux, fish, and development toolchains.

# Development and Validation

## Command Execution

Run ordinary commands, including Git, searches, and installed tools, directly in the normal shell environment.
Use `nix run . -- <command>` for the repository management CLI.
The flake app supplies the CLI's Python environment and tools; no manual dependency installation is needed.
For example, use `nix run . -- hooks` to install the repository hooks.
See `readme.md` for bootstrap and recovery instructions.

## Validation Policy

For routine changes, run `nix run . -- format` (or `nix run . -- format --check`) and `nix run . -- lint`.
Formatting also runs `ruff check --fix --unsafe-fixes`; lint includes strict mypy and full-history gitleaks scanning.
The complete formatter and linter lists live in `dotfiles_py/targets/lint.py`.
Run any checks specific to the changed behavior before finishing.

**Keep Nix configuration evaluation and build checks rare, and only at the end of the entire change set.**
Keep Nix configuration evaluation and build checks rare and at the end of the change set.
When required, the flake check must be the final validation step, after all changes and other checks are complete.
All required checks must pass before the final commit or reporting completion.
If validation requires further edits, rerun the affected checks and keep any required flake check last.
CI runs the same checks; see `.github/workflows/workflow.yml`.

If lint reports that git history is shallow, run `git fetch --unshallow` and rerun lint.
Use this documented workaround rather than investigating alternatives.

# Repository Map and Conventions

- `flake.nix` defines flake outputs; `flake.lock` pins dependencies.
  `nix/tooling.nix` defines the CLI package, default app, and development shells.
- `nix/configuration.nix` and `nix/home.nix` are the system and Home Manager entry points.
  `nix/hosts/` and `nix/users/` hold machine and user definitions; hardware configuration is inlined per host.
- `nix/home-manager/` holds program/category modules, configs, scripts, and dotfiles.
  Neovim's Lua configuration is in `nix/home-manager/text-editors/neovim/config/`.
- `nix/modules/` holds local modules; `nix/overlays/` holds package overlays.
  `nix/packages/` holds standalone packages; `nix/unfree.nix` is the unfree-package allowlist.
- `dotfiles_py/cli.py` defines CLI commands, `targets/` implements them, and `utils.py` provides shared utilities.
  Hooks and scripts live in `dotfiles_py/data/`.

## Nix Conventions

- **Add new Nix and configuration files to the git staging area so the flake can see them.**
- The default package set is stable; `pkgs.unstable` provides packages from a separate input.
- Home Manager configurations cover every configured `user@host` pair and are registered as flake checks.
- `local.home.file` in `nix/modules/home/` links directory trees into `$HOME` one file at a time,
  allowing several modules to populate a shared target directory.

## Overlay Rules

- `nix/overlays/unstable.nix` introduces `pkgs.unstable` from the `nixpkgs-unstable` input
  and auto-loads native overlays from regular `nix/overlays/unstable/*.nix` files.
- Put each `pkgs.unstable` amendment in its own file under `nix/overlays/unstable/`.
  Do not define package-specific overrides directly in `unstable.nix`.
  Each amendment must have the shape `final: prev: { ... }` and must not accept repository arguments.
- `nix/overlays/custom.nix` maps each regular `nix/overlays/custom/<name>.nix` module
  to `pkgs.custom.<name>`.
  Each module must have the shape `final: prev: derivation`.
- The custom loader is not recursive, so keep package modules at the root of `custom/`.
- Store all non-Nix custom package assets under `nix/overlays/custom/scripts/`,
  using package-specific subdirectories where useful.
- Store all package patches in `nix/overlays/patches/` and reference them via `final.locallib.patches + /<name>.patch`.
  `pkgs.unstable` also carries `locallib`, so the same reference works inside `nix/overlays/unstable/`.

# Keyboard Layout and Keymap Design

Design keymaps around shared muscle memory, home-row reachability, and clear ownership between layers.
Use the conventions below when planning shortcuts.
Consult the reference files only for relevant conflicts, exceptions, or implementation details.

## Navigation and Shared Semantics

- Never use plain or modified arrow keys as convenient keymaps or recommend them as ergonomic alternatives.
  Existing arrow aliases may remain, but must not be the only convenient way to perform an action.
- In input contexts, analogous to Vim insert mode, prefer Emacs-style navigation:
  - `Ctrl+B/F` moves backward/forward by character.
  - `Alt+B/F` moves backward/forward by word.
  - `Ctrl+W` deletes the previous word.
  - `Ctrl+P/N` navigates previous/next entries, history items, or completion candidates.
  - `Ctrl+A` moves to the start of the line.
  - Do not assume `Ctrl+E` is available for moving to line end; it is generally used for line scrolling.
- In non-input contexts, analogous to Vim normal mode, prefer Vim-style `hjkl` navigation.
  Do not bind bare letters globally when they would interfere with typing.
- In both contexts, prefer `Ctrl+U/D` for page or half-page navigation and `Ctrl+Y/E` for scrolling up/down by line.
  `Ctrl+B/F` can provide full-page or preview paging in non-input contexts.
- `Ctrl+R` generally has search semantics.
  `Ctrl+C` generally cancels the current operation or exits.
- Prefer consistent meanings across applications rather than preserving conflicting upstream defaults.
  Respect context: text editing, list selection, transcript scrolling, and pane navigation are different operations.
- For additional actions, extend existing application-local leaders and mnemonic groups
  before inventing modifier chords.

## Shortcut Ownership

- Reserve all `Ctrl+Alt+*` and `Shift+Alt+*` combinations for niri, even when a particular chord is currently unbound.
  Existing application-specific exceptions do not make these namespaces available for new shortcuts.
- `Alt+hjkl` belongs to niri window navigation.
  `Ctrl+hjkl` belongs to integrated tmux pane and Neovim split navigation.
  Keep these layers separate; do not reuse their navigation chords for application-local actions.
- `Ctrl+S` is the tmux prefix.
  Preserve the `Alt+Z` resizing sequences used by the Neovim/tmux integration.
- An application binding does not make a shortcut available if the compositor, terminal, or tmux intercepts it first.
  Account for inherited defaults, plugins, and mode-specific bindings when checking a concrete conflict.
- Prefer a reachable, conflict-free application keymap over adding terminal forwarding workarounds.
  Changes to shortcut ownership or cross-layer forwarding require explicit review.

## Custom Layout and Language Support

- Design for the custom `qwerty_rnk` and `jcuken_rnk` layouts, not standard US QWERTY.
  Win keys produce Alt, physical Alt keys provide Level3 symbols, Caps Lock provides Ctrl,
  and right Ctrl provides Super.
- Check the actual gestures needed for punctuation and modifier combinations.
  A mnemonic-looking symbol is not necessarily convenient on this layout.
- Preserve equivalent physical gestures in English and Russian.
  Use the existing generated aliases, tmux alias mechanism, and Neovim language mappings where applicable.
- For generated configurations, edit their `*-overlay.*` sources and regenerate with `nix run . -- configs`.
  Do not maintain generated bindings or Russian aliases manually when an existing generator handles them.

## Cross-Application Conventions

AI tools generally align on `Ctrl+Enter` to submit, Enter to insert a newline,
`Alt+E` for the external editor, and `Alt+V` for image paste.
Preserve these conventions where supported, without assuming every application exposes identical commands or contexts.

Verify that newly chosen modifier combinations remain distinct through Kitty and tmux.
Do not assume that a shortcut accepted by an application's configuration reaches it unchanged.

## Reference Map

Paths below are relative to the repository root.

- Custom keyboard layouts: `nix/keyboard/qwerty_rnk` and `nix/keyboard/jcuken_rnk`.
- niri shortcuts: `nix/home-manager/desktop-envs/configs/.config/niri/config.kdl`.
- Kitty mappings and key forwarding: `nix/home-manager/terminals/configs/.config/kitty/kitty.conf`.
- tmux prefix and plugins: `nix/home-manager/shell/tmux.nix`.
- tmux navigation and forwarding: `nix/home-manager/shell/tmux/tmux.conf`.
- tmux Russian aliases: `nix/overlays/custom/scripts/tmux-russian-keymaps.py`.
- Neovim keymaps and language mappings:

- Neovim plugin-specific bindings:
  `nix/home-manager/text-editors/neovim/config/lua/plugins/configs/`,
  especially `tmux.lua`, `snacks.lua`, `blink.lua`, and `dap.lua`.

# Secrets Management

Secrets in `nix/secrets/` use sops + age with the custom `local.secrets` modules in `nix/modules/secrets/`,
not community `sops-nix`.
Configurations must still evaluate without decrypted secrets.

- `.sops.yaml` defines recipients and encryption rules, including TPM-bound identities.
  Private keys live in `~/.config/sops/` and `/root/.config/sops/`, preserved across reboots by `nix/disk.nix`.
  `nix run . -- updatekeys` in `dotfiles_py/targets/secrets.py` re-encrypts secrets after recipient changes.
- `nix/overlays/custom/scripts/sops-cached.sh` decrypts into `/run/user/$UID/secrets/` (tmpfs), caches results,
  and optionally symlinks them to their target paths.
  System and user decryption services use it.
  Assign secrets with consumer dependencies to a shared `service-name = "decrypt-<consumer>"` group,
  so the consumer waits only for its own secrets instead of the default `decrypt-secrets.service` batch.
  Bootstrap recovery restarts loaded `decrypt-*.service` and `merge-*.service` groups.
- `nix/overlays/locallib/with_secrets.nix` uses `bash_secrets.nix` to inject decrypted environment variables at launch.
  This wrapper is used by all AI CLI tools and Neovim.
- The pre-commit hook blocks plaintext secret filenames and scans the staged diff with gitleaks.
  AI tools are denied access to secrets directories,
  unless user explicitly and proactively allows it for the current task.
  In that case decrypt only the necessary files, do not display secret values, and do not persist plaintext in the repository.
  `nix/overlays/sops.nix` runs the secret editor with `unshare --net` and restricted vim.

# Code Style Guidelines

- **Python**: Strict mypy, ruff with "ALL" rules (see pyproject.toml ignores), 120 char line length, no docstrings for most functions
- **Nix**: nixfmt with --strict, statix linting
- **Shell**: shellcheck, shfmt (2-space indents from .editorconfig)
- **Markdown**: 180 char line length, HTML allowed
- **YAML**: 120 char line length, no document-start
- **Lua**: stylua (2-space indents)
- **KDL**: kdlfmt

# Human in the Way

Apply this workflow only to the root agent, not subagents.
Keep it active for the current task until completion or explicit cancellation.
The root agent owns every user-facing review gate; do not ask subagents to run this workflow themselves.
Respect the host agent's permissions and repository rules, except for the partial-commit exception below.

The optional [workflow diagram](references/workflow.md) illustrates the review cycle for the user.
The instructions here are sufficient; reading the diagram is not required.

## Approval Gates

Approval must be explicit and apply to the presented version and current gate.
Approval of architecture does not approve a step plan; approval of a step plan does not approve its implementation.
Silence, a question, requested revisions, or a general instruction to continue is not approval.
Do not require a particular literal approval word when the user's intent is unambiguous.

At every review gate, end the turn after presenting the material.
**STOP HERE. Do not proceed until the user has explicitly APPROVED the presented version.**
If the user requests revisions, revise the material and stop for review again.
Never treat requested changes as approval of the revised result.

## 1. High-Level Design

Perform a /deep-research of the existing implementation and think through the whole implementation and architecture.
Resolve relevant requirements, compatibility, failure handling, dependencies, and validation decisions with the user.
Determine a best-effort logical commit sequence, separating structural refactoring, supporting functionality,
feature implementation, and integration where those stages have useful work.
The sequence may be amended as understanding improves.

Present the architecture, responsibilities, interactions, API boundaries, and intended commit sequence for review.
Proactively use diagrams, type-hinted Python API sketches, and implementation pseudocode outlines.
Python is for readability; it need not match the project's implementation language.
Pseudocode outlines should sketch major operations, control flow, and boundaries, not complete implementations.
Start with ASCII diagrams; use Mermaid or Typst only when greater complexity warrants them.
Architectural prose may be substantial where useful, but favor diagrams, API boundaries, and implementation outlines.

**STOP HERE. Do not proceed until the user has explicitly APPROVED the presented design.**
Repeat the design review until approved.

Record the approved version in the project in a separate, movable documentation commit before implementing steps.
Keep this commit isolated from production changes so it can be amended or relocated later.
If repository writes are not permitted, wait until they are permitted before recording it or implementing steps.

## 2. Step-Design Review

Begin with a small `Step X/N` header.
N may be approximate; briefly explain changes to the estimate between steps.
Design the next cohesive, independently reviewable change within the approved architecture.
A step may cover part of a commit, one commit, or several commits, such as independent mechanical refactors.
State the intended commit boundaries and relevant validation checks.

Limit each step to 500 lines of meaningful production-code changes across the whole step, not per commit.
Exclude lines belonging to tests, documentation, data, lockfiles, configuration, and other support files from this count.
Those files and activities remain part of the step and must be planned, implemented, and reviewed where relevant.
Also 500LOC rule do not apply to **separated** steps only containing unchanged moved code and formatting-only changes.
Do not use net line growth to hide a large change or classify production logic as support material to bypass the limit.
If implementation would exceed the budget, stop and obtain approval for a revised split before continuing.

Keep the plan focused: aim for no more than 2 A4 pages.
Lead with diagrams, Python-style API sketches, and implementation pseudocode outlines; keep text notes minimal.
Do not present full implementations, even as pseudocode.

**STOP HERE. Do not proceed until the user has explicitly APPROVED the presented step plan.**
Repeat the step-design review until approved.

## 3. Implementation Review

Implement only the approved step and run its agreed validation checks.
Embed concise documentation only for critical context that cannot be inferred from the code,
including interaction diagrams where useful.
Do not copy step plans into obvious comments or docstrings.

Commit at the planned boundaries and keep each commit focused and usable.
When a step covers only part of a planned commit, leave it uncommitted for review of the working diff.

# Fingerprint sensor security — summary

Core principle: a fingerprint is an identifier, not a secret — it cannot be rotated and you leave copies everywhere, including on the device itself.
Every sane design therefore uses the match only as a gate in front of a real cryptographic secret.

## 1. MoC vs MoH

- **Match-on-host (MoH)**: the sensor is a camera; it ships images to the OS, which stores templates on disk and matches in software.
  Templates and matching live inside the attackable OS.
- **Match-on-chip (MoC)**: the sensor's own microcontroller stores templates in its flash and matches internally; templates never leave the chip.
  The host receives only a verdict — which is worthless unless the channel is authenticated, since anything on the bus can say "yes".
- Modern laptop sensors are typically MoC.

## 2. How MoC enrollment and matching work

- Enrollment: finger is scanned several times, the template is assembled and stored inside the sensor under a template ID.
- The host (fprintd) keeps only a bookkeeping record: "user U, finger F → template #N on sensor serial S" (~150 bytes, no biometric data).
- Matching: host asks "verify against template #N"; the chip captures, matches internally, answers matched / not matched.
- This pinning to a recorded template ID protects against attacking with side-loaded keys to sensor (i.e. using a live OS).
  The new template gets a fresh ID that no host record references, so an identify-then-check-ID verify rejects it.
- Without an authenticated channel this bookkeeping is mostly useless.
  If the attacker learns the victim's template-ID string (some sensors allow to read it from chip), they can delete it
  and re-enroll their own finger forcing the same ID, which every host record already trusts.

## 3. How the OS verifies login with SDCP (Windows model)

SDCP = Microsoft's Secure Device Connection Protocol; spec is public.

- **Factory**: vendor burns a unique per-device ECDSA key into the sensor, certified via a chain up to the vendor root;
  immutable boot ROM measures and attests sensor firmware.
- **Pairing (every connection)**: host challenges; sensor answers with cert chain, firmware attestation, and a signature by its factory key over an ECDH exchange.
  Host verifies the chain, both derive a session key; all further sensor messages are MAC'd with it.
  Defeats fake/impersonated hardware and bus MitM. Certificates prove *class* (genuine sensor), the session binding proves *instance*.
- **Enrollment**: "created template #N" arrives sealed, and #N is a MAC over a sensor nonce under the session secret, not a host-chosen value.
- **Login**: host sends a fresh nonce; sensor answers sealed: "nonce + template #N matched".
  Freshness kills replay; naming #N kills maliciously added templates; the seal kills spoofed devices.
- A sensor swapped from an identical laptop passes the certificate check (it is genuine) but fails instance binding: host records name the original device identity,
  and under SDCP that identity is the factory key, which cannot be faked. Result is fallback to password, not a breach.

## 4. Current state on Linux

- **Today**: no SDCP. fprintd talks plaintext USB and trusts any device that claims to be the sensor; no nonce, no seal, no identity proof.
  Device binding is by self-reported serial — honest-hardware bookkeeping only.
  The verdict is reduced to a yes/no over D-Bus to PAM, and a match unlocks nothing cryptographic: keyring stays locked, LUKS/sops have separate TPM paths.
  Trust chain: PAM → root daemon (faith) → any alleged sensor (faith) → finger.
- **In progress**: SDCP host support exists in community forks (EgisTec `egismoc`) and Ubuntu's libfprint TOD fork (1.95.0+tod1, Feb 2026); upstream MR pending.
  Driven by necessity: newest EgisTec firmware refuses to persist enrollments without SDCP.
- **After SDCP lands**: the sensor→fprintd hop becomes real crypto; the fprintd→PAM hop stays a boolean, and the TPM remains uninvolved.
  For the login gate itself that is rough parity with non-enclave Windows; the remaining gaps (enclave for the middleman, secrets behind the gate) are about what login *yields*.

## 5. Strong sensor \<-> TPM connection

Goal: no software in the trusted path — the TPM itself verifies that a match just happened, so even kernel-level malware cannot forge an unseal.
The TPM is not on the USB bus and verifies only proofs made with key material it was given in advance; hence the sensor must persistently hold a key the TPM can check.

Two equivalent schemes:

1. **Asymmetric**: register the sensor's public key in the TPM; per match, the sensor signs "TPM nonce + matched identity"; TPM verifies via `PolicySigned` and unseals.
   Clean provisioning (no secret changes hands), but no firmware exposes per-match signatures — the factory key signs only during pairing, which attests presence, not a match.
   Also: ECDSA is expensive for the MCU, the factory key is unrotatable and a permanent identifier.
1. **Symmetric (what Windows ships as "secure sensors")**: on first sight the OS generates a secret, installs one copy in the sensor and one in the TPM, then forgets it.
   Per login: OS obtains a nonce from the TPM, passes it to the sensor; on match the sensor returns HMAC(secret, nonce + matched user identity); the OS relays it;
   the TPM recomputes the HMAC with its copy and unseals. The HMAC expires in seconds.
   HMAC is the TPM's native session-authorization language, nearly free on the MCU, and the shared secret *is* the instance pairing (a swapped sensor holds no valid secret).
   The OS is a one-time matchmaker and thereafter a courier that cannot forge.

Both require the signed/MAC'd message to contain the TPM's nonce (freshness) and the matched identity (pins to templates that existed at seal time).
Requires the "secure sensor" tier: matching in an isolated environment, secure sample input, secure credential release, presentation-attack detection.
Premium subset of sensors only; plain SDCP sensors fall back to the OS-trusting path.

## 6. What Linux lacks to implement scheme 2

Everything host-side already exists: measured boot + PCR policies, `tpm2-tools` HMAC-key import, HMAC session authorization, SDCP (in progress).
No kernel work — all userspace. Missing are exactly two sensor operations (Windows driver API names; per-vendor USB wire protocol undocumented):

1. `CreateKey` — "store this long-term secret".
1. `IdentifyFeatureSetSecure` — "match; on success return HMAC(secret, nonce + matched identity)".

Path to implementation: check the sensor reports `WINBIO_CAPABILITY_SECURE_SENSOR` under Windows, sniff the Windows driver's provisioning and secure-match traffic,
decode two message types, add to the libfprint driver, plus a small helper that seals TPM secrets under HMAC-session policy.
Nobody is publicly working on this tier; adjacent reverse engineering (python-validity, Goodix SPI, egismoc SDCP) proves feasibility.
Fallback without secure-sensor firmware: reuse the SDCP session key as the TPM-shared secret —
weaker custody (root present at pairing can copy it), still better than a D-Bus boolean.

## 7. Brute-force protection on the sensor — missing

- Consumer sensors target FAR ≈ 1/50,000 per attempt; physical presentation (fabricate + press a fake finger per try) is the only real rate limiter.
  A lifted print (off the laptop chassis itself) beats brute force anyway.
- Electronic image injection is blocked by MoC packaging (imaging array wired directly to the matcher, no "match this image" command) — not by any lockout.
- Throttling: phones keep an escalating lockout counter in the secure world, surviving reboots.
  On PCs the lockout is conventionally the host's job (Windows counts failures and falls back to PIN) — useless against a stolen sensor, since the attacker brings their own host.
  Microsoft's secure-sensor spec does *not* mandate anti-hammering.
- Empirical result (one laptop MoC sensor, 60 consecutive false attempts via `fprintd-verify`): flat latency, no lockout, no errors — **no firmware anti-hammering**.
  Irrelevant today (a stolen sensor unlocks nothing), but it becomes the weak link under scheme 2, where the chip would hold the TPM-shared secret.

## One-line trust chains

- **Windows secure-sensor tier**: TPM \<-> sensor share a secret directly (OS introduced them once, then forgot) → sensor trusts finger. OS is a courier.
- **Windows default / post-SDCP Linux goal**: TPM ← measured OS ← factory-signed sensor ← finger;
  the OS is the trusted joint (Windows armors it with a VBS enclave; Linux has a root daemon).
- **Linux today**: nothing ← root daemon ← any alleged sensor ← finger; a match releases no secret at all.

- Merge only PRs I explicitly approve, using rebase merge only.
- Immediately before merging, verify the PR is still open and its current head has passing required checks.
  Missing, pending, or cancelled required checks are not success.
- Match the expected head commit when merging.
  Never bypass branch protection or use administrator overrides.
- Recheck remaining PRs after merges.
  Earlier passing results do not guarantee compatibility with newly merged updates.

## Investigate remaining PRs

- Work in `~/projects/<repository>`.
  If absent, clone using SSH.
- Read repository instructions and inspect Git status before switching branches.
  Preserve existing changes, untracked files, and local-only commits.
  If switching would endanger existing work, pause and ask.
- Check out the Dependabot branch for each PR requiring investigation.
- Investigate actual failure causes before proposing changes.
  Inspect dependency changes, tool versions, upstream source, and macro expansions where relevant.
- Search upstream issues and fixes.
  Distinguish merged fixes from fixes actually available in the pinned dependencies.
- Propose the smallest reasonable compatibility fix that preserves intended behavior.
  Follow decision-review requirements before resolving behavioral or design choices.
- Do not blindly apply linter suggestions, weaken checks, or introduce workarounds solely to make CI green.
  For upstream regressions, offer skipping the update when appropriate.

## Fix history and validation

- Put compatibility fixes before the dependency update:
  `existing base → compatibility fix → dependency update`.
- Validate the fix with the original dependencies, then replay the update and validate again.
  Each commit should represent a correct, usable state.
- Preserve the dependency-update patch unless an approved change requires otherwise.
- Run repository-required checks and focused checks for the changed behavior.
  Continue beyond the first repaired diagnostic to uncover further failures.
- Fold corrections into the relevant fix commit and replay the update.
  Do not leave temporary fixup commits.
- Record HEAD before the first rewrite in each repository.
  Preserve unrelated work throughout history changes.

- Present another review table after investigation and local fixes.
  Include repository, PR link, original failure, fix or recommendation,
  validation results, remaining blockers, and push status.
- Wait for my review and explicit merge approval.

- Rebase-merge approved PRs only after all required checks pass.

- Repeat investigation and review until every PR has an agreed disposition.
- Skipping means leaving the PR open and unmerged.
